Vengeance, aka "revenge," is wrong and there is no part that cannot be easily replaced of revenge. Essentially, it is an entirely unnecessary evil. Shit, I don't really want to put forth the entire argument right here and now, so I'll do a half-baked version. If you want me to come back later and edit this just say so (I'm about to hit the sack).

So, this argument does not say that murder etc is wrong- only revenge. Killing in self defense is not an issue of morality, but rather an issue of ability (and the laws on the issue are fucked up at the moment; I hope that laws change to allow warning shots and shooting not to kill, but because it's easy to sue for that you'll never find that happening). Namely, when you enter the moral argument of whose life should be taken, your's or the aggressors, you assume that the aggressor is worth less than you. While this judgement has high probability of holding true you must make the realization that this is an assumption: it is not absolute fact. Don't get me wrong, it is not a "wrong" assumption to make by any stretch of the imagination, but it absolutely is an assumption.

In this moment of life or death you are not given the clarity to understand your attacker nor the ability to rationalize and compare values of potential each person could contribute to society. In stead of this menial task we simply make the assumption that the attacker is worth less due to their current course of action. Again, this is an okay assumption to take: it is unreasonable to expect all members of the population to have the cognitive abilities nor the patience to take such an action and, further, supporting a position to expect members to take allow their lives to be taken would only serve enable murderers to rise without granting any benefit.

Now that we've thoroughly established that self-defense is not wrong we can now discuss why revenge is wrong.

In the previous situation the question about whose life would be taken is considered, but in revenge there is no such choice: only one life can be taken of the two choices. The happenings of the past have no bearing on this issue. Reasonably, an objection is raised stating that this will enable murderers, but one does not need revenge to do so.

Again, in that previous situation, an assumption of value to society is made by dismissing it- an okay assumption, but one that you must realize is not a rational judgement. Assumptions in moments of frenzy must adhere to previously established moral anchors (feelings of ethics are neurologically a faster method of thinking than considering the predicament) meaning that outside of this moment we are given the luxury of not making this assumption. In this moment we can sit down and make the considerations; as it is no longer a choice between who of two people will be killed you are merely assessing whether a person's impact on society is positive or negative.

However, there in lies the problem: there is such a thing as a non-repeat murderer. Whether by coincidence (which we should not count on) or because we have properly educated the murderer they have chosen not to murder again and will continue this choice onward into the future. It is entirely possible that the person is a net-gain for society, but you still do not want them to be a repeat murderer, so what do you do?

When asking questions of "what is true justice" you must understand that justice isn't about punishing people. Punishing people doesn't matter- emotions are worthless. What does matter are the outcomes of our choices culminating in an endless march; whereby doing good constantly progresses us towards the desired result. So, again, as emotions are worthless we do not consider the grieving people demanding vengeance: we have no need to. Instead, we attempt to turn the murderer into a productive member of society attempting to, at the least, allow them the same level of productivity they had held previously, and also hoping that they will become more productive.
